title: "What Is That in Your Hand?"
paragraphs:
"What Is That in Your Hand?"
The Ordinary Thing God Uses to Rewrite Extraordinary Lives
There are questions in Scripture that echo through history like thunder rolling across mountains. They are not merely questions asked in a moment—they are invitations that expose the human heart.
One of those questions is breathtaking in its simplicity:
"What is that in your hand?"
It was not asked because God lacked information.
It was asked because Moses lacked understanding.
And perhaps... so do we.

Long before miracles shook Egypt, before the Red Sea split into towering walls of water, before manna fell from heaven, before a nation found freedom, there was a broken shepherd standing before a burning bush.
Not a prince.
Not a hero.
Not a confident leader.
Just a man who believed his greatest story was already behind him.

Moses had once imagined himself as Israel's deliverer. Raised in Pharaoh's palace, educated in all the wisdom of Egypt, powerful in speech and action (Acts 7:22), he likely believed God would use his strength, influence, education, and position.
Instead...
Everything collapsed.
One impulsive act.
One murdered Egyptian.
One lifetime of regret.
Forty years disappeared into the wilderness.
Forty years of silence.
Forty years of wondering whether God had forgotten him.
Many people know what that wilderness feels like.
Perhaps you've watched opportunities disappear because of your own mistakes.
Perhaps shame has whispered that your usefulness expired years ago.
Perhaps everyone remembers the scandal, but nobody remembers the tears you cried afterward.
Maybe you've convinced yourself that your greatest purpose died with your greatest failure.
Yet Scripture keeps telling a different story.
Because the Gospel has always been about one breathtaking truth:
Jesus specializes in rewriting lives that everyone else has finished reading.
That is why our theme is not merely a slogan.
The God who called Moses still calls broken people today.
When Moses stood before the bush that burned yet was not consumed (Exodus 3:2), God did not begin by discussing military strategy.
He did not hand Moses a sword.
He did not recruit an army.
Instead, He asked an almost strangely ordinary question.

"וַיֹּאמֶר אֵלָיו יְהוָה מַה־זֶּה בְיָדֶךָ"
Vayyōmer ēlāyw YHWH, mah-zeh beyādekha?
"And the LORD said to him, 'What is that in your hand?'" (Exodus 4:2)
The Hebrew phrase מַה־זֶּה בְיָדֶךָ (mah-zeh beyādekha) literally means:
"What is this in your hand?"
It sounds almost too simple.
Almost insignificant.
But God often begins with ordinary questions because He intends to reveal extraordinary truths.
Moses answered honestly.
"A staff."
Nothing more.
Not a royal scepter.
Not a weapon forged for battle.
Not a symbol of greatness.
Just a shepherd's staff.
The Hebrew word is מַטֶּה (matteh).
It refers to a rod, a walking stick, a shepherd's staff, but it also came to symbolize authority, leadership, and even the identity of an entire tribe of Israel.
To Moses, however, it was simply another ordinary tool used every single day.
He leaned on it.
Walked with it.
Worked with it.
Nothing about it appeared miraculous.
That is exactly the point.
God rarely begins His greatest works with what impresses people.
He begins with what people overlook.
Throughout Scripture, God repeatedly chooses the ordinary to reveal His extraordinary glory.
David carried a sling.
A widow carried a little oil.
A boy carried five loaves and two fish.
The disciples carried empty nets.
Mary carried an impossible promise.
The apostles carried nothing but the Gospel.
And Jesus Himself carried a cross.
Heaven delights in transforming ordinary things into testimonies that only God can explain.
The question was never about the staff.
The question was about surrender.
God already knew what Moses possessed.
Moses needed to discover that what had been in his hand all along could become powerful only after it was placed into God's hand.
This pattern reaches its ultimate fulfillment in Jesus Christ.
Humanity stretched out empty hands in rebellion.
Christ stretched out pierced hands in redemption.
Where Adam grasped for what was forbidden, Jesus surrendered Himself completely to the Father's will.
The Apostle Paul writes:
The cross looked like defeat.
It appeared to be scandal.
Public shame.
Mockery.
Rejection.
Failure.
Yet the resurrection revealed that what looked like history's greatest scandal became heaven's greatest display of grace.
That is the Gospel.
God transforms instruments of shame into instruments of salvation.
He transforms failures into testimonies.
Brokenness into worship.
Sinners into saints.
Enemies into children.
Death into life.
That is why the question still confronts every reader today.
What is in your hand?
Perhaps it is your profession.
Your gifts.
Your painful testimony.
Your artistic talent.
Your business.
Your camera.
Your pen.
Your voice.
Your platform.
Your generosity.
Your home.
Your influence.
Your scars.
Perhaps the very thing you've dismissed as ordinary is the very thing God intends to use for His glory when surrendered completely to Him.
Notice that God did not ask Moses to become someone else before using him.
He asked him to surrender what he already had.
Grace has always worked this way.
God is not searching for flawless people.
He is redeeming surrendered people through Jesus Christ.
The deepest scandal in your life does not surprise the Savior who bore your sins on the cross.
If you are in Christ, your identity is no longer written by your failures but by His finished work.
That is why every believer can say with confidence:
"My past explains me, but it no longer defines me."
Only Jesus has the authority to rewrite the ending.
And He still does.
Maybe you've been asking God for something spectacular while overlooking what He has already placed in your hands.
Maybe your miracle begins not with receiving something new, but with surrendering something familiar.
The Gospel never minimizes human weakness.
It magnifies God's power working through surrendered weakness.
As Paul wrote:
"But we have this treasure in jars of clay, to show that the surpassing power belongs to God and not to us." (2 Corinthians 4:7)
The treasure has never been the jar.
The glory has always belonged to Christ.

If this message reminded you that God can still redeem ordinary lives for extraordinary purposes, don't let it stop with you. Your testimony may become the encouragement another believer desperately needs.
Because when you support work that faithfully proclaims Christ, you're not purchasing a product—you are partnering in making His name known.
One surrendered hand in the hands of an Almighty Savior can change generations.
